question: Why can the line from initialization to a successfully trained deep network stay at random-guess loss and error for most of its length, and does that plateau reveal anything about optimization difficulty?

key_findings.claim: A last-layer bias gap plus depth and small initialization can produce a long random-guessing plateau even when training itself succeeds.
key_findings.evidence: For an r-layer ReLU or linear fully connected network with zero initial output bias, bounded endpoint weights, balanced classes, and a positive trained gap between the largest and second-largest output biases, Theorem 1 gives an interval where every example is predicted as the largest-bias class and error equals 1-1/k. It also bounds early cross-entropy near log(k). The weight signal scales roughly as alpha^r while the last bias scales as alpha, so the plateau length grows with depth under the stated bounds.

anchors.section: Plateau for loss and error interpolations
Proof for deep fully connected networks

key_findings.claim: A balanced dataset does not force equal trained biases: the paper's homogeneous toy model learns classes sequentially and leaves the last-learned class with the largest bias.
key_findings.evidence: For f_i(x)=<W_i,x>^r+b_i on orthogonal class means plus Gaussian noise, small random initialization and cross-entropy gradient flow, Theorem 2 proves zero training error and an order-one bias gap with high probability under explicit dimension, sample, noise, and time conditions. The induction shows that once a class is learned its bias falls while unlearned classes remain near the maximum, so initialization differences determine a class-learning order.

anchors.section: Training dynamics for creating a bias gap

key_findings.claim: In the homogeneous model, the authors prove both plateau ranges and eventual monotonicity rather than only a qualitative scaling argument.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 supplies an error interval fixed at 1-1/k, shows error is non-increasing after a small alpha threshold, bounds the early loss near log(k), and proves late loss is strictly decreasing. The proof tracks when the alpha^r class signal overtakes each alpha-scaled trained bias gap.

anchors.section: Plateau and monotonicity for the r-homogeneous-weight network

key_findings.claim: Bias ablations, homogeneous bias interpolation, initialization scaling, and depth sweeps support the proposed mechanism across MNIST-family and CIFAR experiments, but bias mainly explains the error plateau rather than the entire loss curve.
key_findings.evidence: On deep fully connected nets and VGG models, removing biases or interpolating a layer-h bias as alpha^h b(T) greatly shortens the error plateau while leaving loss curves comparatively similar. Smaller output-scale initialization and greater depth lengthen both error and loss plateaus. Per-class learning order often tracks final output-bias order on small MNIST subsets, although the appendix presents a correlated-class counterexample.

key_findings.claim: Monotonic linear interpolation is not a certificate of easy optimization, and a non-monotonic slice is not a certificate of hardness.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A constructs an NP-hard tensor optimization problem whose line from a fixed initialization to its minimizer is convex and monotonically decreasing, and a two-dimensional objective for which gradient flow reaches the unique global minimizer from every nonzero start while a positive-measure set of initialization-to-minimum lines is non-monotonic.

Easy function with non-monotonic loss interpolation

method.core_idea: Separate the homogeneity degree of the weight-dependent signal from that of additive biases along a parameter-space interpolation, prove the resulting plateau in deep and stylized models, and intervene on those degrees empirically.
method.mechanism: Along theta(alpha)=(1-alpha)theta(0)+alpha theta(T), a depth-r product of small-to-trained weights contributes approximately alpha^r, while an output bias initialized at zero contributes alpha. A trained class-bias gap therefore dominates logits until alpha is close enough to one. A separate gradient-flow analysis explains how sequential class learning can generate the required bias gap even with perfectly balanced labels.
assumptions: The deep-network plateau theorem assumes an r-layer, r>=3, fully connected linear or ReLU network with bias only at the output, balanced classes, bounded input norms, small layerwise initialization norms, bounded trained norms, and a positive trained bias gap.

The dynamics theorem uses the stylized output f_i(x)=<W_i,x>^r+b_i, orthonormal class means with small Gaussian noise, absolute-Gaussian initialization, continuous-time gradient flow, cross-entropy, and constant class count.
High dimension and sample size scale polynomially in inverse initialization according to the theorem, while noise is sufficiently small.
Empirical interpolation uses the specific coordinate parameterization; it is not invariant to layer rescaling or equivalent-network symmetries.
Training-set loss and error along one line are treated as descriptive observables, not complete summaries of the surrounding landscape.

techniques.role: Contrasts alpha^r weight signal with alpha-scaled output bias along the interpolation.
Turns endpoint norm and class-bias assumptions into explicit random-guess error and loss intervals.
Proves that small random advantages cause classes to be learned one by one and create unequal biases.
Changes a layer-h bias path from alpha to alpha^h to experimentally remove the degree mismatch.
Formally decouples slice shape from computational or gradient-flow difficulty.
Tests the predicted direction of plateau changes on fully connected and convolutional networks.

evaluations.setting: Depth-10 width-1024 ReLU fully connected networks on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST
evaluations.metric: Training loss and error at 50 points from initialization to the 100-epoch SGD endpoint
evaluations.result: Last-layer or all-layer biases create much longer error plateaus than no bias; homogeneous bias interpolation sharply shortens them, while loss curves change less.
evaluations.baseline: Ordinary coordinate-wise linear interpolation with and without trainable biases

evaluations.setting: VGG-16 without batch normalization on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
evaluations.metric: Interpolation plateau length under bias and path ablations
evaluations.result: The qualitative bias and homogeneous-interpolation effects transfer to convolutional networks and harder datasets, including plateaus under standard initialization in some CIFAR-100 settings.
evaluations.baseline: VGG trained with ordinary bias interpolation

evaluations.result: Smaller initialization consistently lengthens both plateau types in the reported MNIST-family and CIFAR experiments.
Deeper models show longer plateaus, matching the high-order alpha scaling prediction.
evaluations.baseline: Shallower model in each architecture family

evaluations.setting: Balanced two- and three-class MNIST subsets
evaluations.metric: Per-class training loss timing and output-bias trajectories
evaluations.result: Later-learned classes usually acquire larger biases, but a {7,8,9} example reverses the last two because cross-class softmax correlations affect bias derivatives.

limitations: The fully connected theorem assumes the trained bias gap rather than deriving it for real deep ReLU networks.
The derived bias gap uses a nonstandard polynomial homogeneous model, orthogonal class features, small Gaussian noise, absolute initialization, gradient flow, and asymptotic scaling conditions.
Empirical results use three seeds, 50 interpolation points, training metrics, four vision datasets, and only FCN/VGG families without batch normalization.
Bias removal explains the error plateau strongly but has limited effect on the observed loss plateau, so other mechanisms remain.
The interpolation depends on a particular parameterization; rescaling adjacent layers or changing bias coordinates can alter the curve without altering the represented endpoints.
No direct measure of actual optimization time, basin volume, generalization, or off-line curvature is predicted by plateau length.
failure_modes: A largest output bias can make the entire early line predict one class even though the trained model is accurate, producing an alarming but optimization-irrelevant plateau.
Correlated classes can violate the toy rule that the last-learned class has the largest final bias.
Batch normalization, residual paths, intermediate biases, and feature shortcuts can introduce lower-degree alpha terms that break the simple alpha^r calculation.
Sparse sampling of alpha can miss narrow barriers or apparent non-monotonicity near either endpoint.
Coordinate reparameterization can create or remove a plateau, so comparing curves across architectures may confound geometry with parameter units.
Monotonicity can coexist with NP-hard global optimization and non-monotonicity with easy gradient flow, invalidating hardness inferences from either alone.
reusable_insights: Decompose an interpolation by the pathwise homogeneity degree of each computational route before interpreting its shape.
Intervene on biases and initialization scale, not only weights, when diagnosing loss-landscape slices.
Plot per-class logits, errors, and bias trajectories; aggregate loss can hide a one-class prediction plateau.
Use function-space or symmetry-normalized paths alongside raw parameter interpolation because slice shape is coordinate dependent.
Validate any claimed optimization proxy against constructed counterexamples and direct training-cost measurements.
Distinguish sufficient endpoint conditions for a plateau from a theory explaining why ordinary training creates those endpoints.
open_questions: What mechanisms explain the loss plateau after homogeneous bias interpolation removes most of the error plateau?
Can a bias-gap theorem be proved for realistic ReLU, convolutional, residual, and normalized networks on correlated data?
Which interpolation geometry is invariant to common neural-network reparameterizations and predicts actual optimizer behavior?
How do weight decay, adaptive optimizers, label imbalance, calibration, and large-scale pretraining change class-bias dynamics?
Can finite-depth path diagnostics be combined with neighborhoods or multi-dimensional subspaces to produce a validated optimization-difficulty measure?
Does plateau length predict any downstream property once depth, initialization, and bias scale are controlled?

competitive_landscape.title: Qualitatively Characterizing Neural Network Optimization Problems
competitive_landscape.difference: Goodfellow, Vinyals, and Saxe use approximately convex monotone MNIST slices to argue that encountered optimization paths are simple; the reviewed paper proves that a similarly simple slice can be computationally uninformative and explains why modern deep slices can have plateaus.

competitive_landscape.title: Revisiting 'Qualitatively Characterizing Neural Network Optimization Problems'
competitive_landscape.difference: Frankle documents high-until-late loss and error on modern CIFAR-10 and ImageNet models and questions the earlier easy-optimization conclusion; this paper supplies a bias/depth/initialization mechanism, theorem, and intervention for that observation.

competitive_landscape.title: Analyzing Monotonic Linear Interpolation in Neural Network Loss Landscapes
competitive_landscape.difference: Lucas et al. relate parameter lines to function-space Gaussian length and give sufficient monotonicity conditions, with formal control mainly near NTK linearization; the reviewed work targets the unexplained plateau and emphasizes unequal homogeneity of biases and deep weight signals.

competitive_landscape.title: What can linear interpolation of neural network loss landscapes tell us?
competitive_landscape.difference: Vlaar and Frankle systematically vary data, initialization, optimizer, architecture, and layers and find slice shape does not track test accuracy; the reviewed paper reaches a compatible caution through explicit hardness counterexamples and a specific bias-driven plateau theory.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: the paper's strongest novelty is explaining a concrete modern MLI anomaly with unequal pathwise homogeneity and turning that explanation into a clean homogeneous-bias intervention. Its formal counterexamples decisively undercut the use of one-dimensional slice shape as an optimization-hardness certificate. The gradient-flow derivation of a bias gap is technically substantial but stylized, and the empirical fact that bias interventions barely change the loss plateau means the mechanism is an important partial account rather than a complete landscape theory.
